items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to high school diploma
requirements
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1983

SPONSOR: GOUNARDES
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the education law, in relation to high school diploma
requirements

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to create a new requirement for high school
graduation under the Education Law; requiring a student to either
complete and submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid
(FAFSA), or complete a waiver stating the student understands what the
FAFSA is and has chosen not to file an application. This bill also
creates a requirement for high schools to notify students at least four
times a year about state-sponsored scholarships, financial aid, and
other available assistance.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 amends Section 305 of the Education Law to require the commis-
sioner to promulgate rules and regulations to require the parent or
guardian, or if the student is eighteen years old, the student them-
selves, to either complete a FAFSA application or complete a waiver
stating that they understand what the FAFSA is and have chosen not to
file an application.

Section 1 also requires each school district to submit an annual report
to the Commissioner of Education on the total number of FAFSAs completed
in the prior year, the total number of waivers completed, the total
number of senior year students in the prior academic year, and the total
number of anticipated senior year students in the coming year.

This section also requires each school district with at least one high
school to provide each eligible high school student, and if applicable
their parent or guardian, any support or assistance necessary for
compliance of the regulations set forth, and to create a uniform waiver
form, to be made available in English and the twelve most common non-
English languages in this state.

Finally, section one requires the commissioner to promulgate rules and
regulations requiring each high school to give each high school senior
and junior explanations of state-sponsored scholarships, financial aid
and assistance available to students attending college or post-secondary
educational institutions.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

In the United States today, an estimated 43 million Americans collec-
tively owe $1.5 trillion in student debt - a figure that continues to
rise. As a result, most high school graduates weigh the value of a
college degree against the prospect of entering the workforce tens or
even hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt. On August 9, 2019, the
New York Times reported findings by the National College Access Network
(NCAN), a nonprofit group that promotes post-high school education. NCAN
discovered that students who complete the Free Application for Federal
Student Aid (FAFSA) are significantly more likely to continue their

studies after high school. Moreover, this correlation is particularly
strong amongst low-income students who need financial aid the most.

In addition to educating students about their available financial aid
options, filling out a FAFSA spurs high school seniors to consider
pursuing a college or post-secondary degree. This legislation includes
an opt-out option that ensures non-college-bound students won't be
barred from graduation for not filling out a FAFSA. For example, a high
school graduate who is immediately entering the armed forces will not be
required to fill out a FAFSA and can complete a waiver instead.

Other states have enacted similar laws. Beginning in the 2017-18 school
year, Louisiana required students to complete the FAFSA. The state now
leads the nation with nearly 79% of its high school seniors completing
the FAFSA compared to only 44% in 2013. Alabama, California, Illinois,
New Hampshire, Texas have also adopted such policies. Maryland does not
require students to file the FAFSA, but rather it obligates local educa-
tional agencies to encourage and assist as many high school seniors as
possible in completing and submitting the FAFSA. Colorado establishes a
grant program for local educational agencies who adopt a requirement to
assist students in FAFSA completion. States recognize the importance of
completing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid that is corre-
lated with positive postsecondary student outcomes, such as enrollment
after high school graduation and persistence.This legislation would help
New York achieve similar success.

The FAFSA can be difficult to complete, especially if a student's
parents or guardians are unable to help. This bill addresses that by
requiring high schools to provide assistance to students and parents in
filling out either a FAFSA or a waiver. It also requires the Commission-
er of Education to create rules and regulations to require school
districts with at least one high school to provide the necessary support
or assistance for compliance.

Currently, too many New York students are unaware of the Excelsior
Program, which provides free tuition for eligible full-time students at
CUNY and SUNY two-year and four-year colleges. In many cases, these
students are missing opportunities because their guidance counselors
fail to promote these scholarships.

New York students should graduate high school with all the available
tools and resources needed to attend college or post-secondary educa-
tional institutions with as little debt as possible. This bill works
towards that purpose by requiring each high school to notify its seniors
and juniors about state-sponsored scholarships, financial aid, and
assistance during the school year.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2021-22: S5409 - Referred to education

2019-20: A8566 - Referred to education

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

TBD

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the first of July two years after the date
on which it shall have become a law.

AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to notice of post-secondary
financial aid programs

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1983AREVISED 6/1/23

SPONSOR: GOUNARDES
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the education law, in relation to notice of post-secon-
dary financial aid programs

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to require all schools to present on post-
secondary financial aid opportunities such as the Free Application for
Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or a DREAM Act application and for students
to complete an affidavit indicating if they will be applying for such
aid.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill adds a new Part VI to Article 14 of the Education
Law to require the Higher Education Services Corporation (HESC) to
create a uniform presentation on FAFSA and DREAM, which will be
presented to all students throughout the state.

Each high school senior shall then be required to complete an affidavit
affirming that they have either attended the presentation or received
the presentation materials and if they intend to apply for FAFSA or
DREAM (which shall be coupled together in one category on the form) or
neither type of aid.

The Commissioner of Education shall be responsible for creating the
affidavit form which shall be made available in the twelve most common
non-English languages spoken in the state and up to four additional
languages.

Schools shall be responsible for distributing and collecting the affida-
vit forms. Forms shall then be transmitted to the Commissioner along
with data on senior class sizes. The Commissioner shall then transmit
this information to HESC for the purposes of compiling the report in
section 694-f of Education Law.

In section 694-f, HESC shall compile a report on total number of affida-
vits, per school district and statewide, the total number of FAFSA and
DREAM Act applications filed in the previous year and how such numbers
compare to the previous five years, and what effect if any that HESC
believes this act has had on applications filed. The report shall be
delivered to the legislature and published online on an annual basis.

Finally, the Commissioner and HESC shall create a uniform notice
describing FAFSA and DREAM which shall be distributed to all high school
seniors no less than four times a year and high school juniors no less
than two times a year.

Section two sets the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

In the United States today, an estimated 43 million Americans collec-
tively owe $1.5 trillion in student debt - a figure that continues to
rise. As a result, most high school graduates weigh the value of a
college degree against the prospect of entering the workforce tens or
even hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt. On August 9, 2019, the
New York Times reported findings by the National College Access Network
(NCAN), a nonprofit group that promotes post-high school education. NCAN
discovered that students who complete the Free Application for Federal
Student Aid (FAFSA) are significantly more likely to continue their
studies after high school. Moreover, this correlation is particularly
strong amongst low-income students who need financial aid the most.

In addition to educating students about their available financial aid
options, filling out a FAFSA spurs high school seniors to consider
pursuing a college or post-secondary degree. This legislation includes
an opt-out option that ensures non-college-bound students won't be
barred from graduation for not filling out a FAFSA. For example, a high
school graduate who is immediately entering the armed forces will not be
required to fill out a FAFSA and can complete a waiver instead.

Other states have enacted similar laws. Beginning in the 2017-18 school
year, Louisiana required students to complete the FAFSA. The state now
leads the nation with nearly 79% of its high school seniors completing
the FAFSA compared to only 44% in 2013. Alabama, California, Illinois,
New Hampshire, and Texas have also adopted such policies. Maryland does
not require students to file the FAFSA, but rather it obligates local
educational agencies to encourage and assist as many high school seniors
as possible in completing and submitting the FAFSA. Colorado establishes
a grant program for local educational agencies who adopt a requirement
to assist students in FAFSA completion. States recognize the importance
of completing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid that is
correlated with positive postsecondary student outcomes, such as enroll-
ment after high school graduation and persistence.This legislation would
help New York achieve similar success.

New York students should graduate high school with all the available
tools and resources needed to attend college or post-secondary educa-
tional institutions with as little debt as possible. This bill works
towards that purpose by requiring each high school to notify its seniors
and juniors about state-sponsored scholarships, financial aid, and
assistance during the school year and ensuring that they complete an
affidavit detailing if they plan to complete the FAFSA, a DREAM Act
application, or neither type of aid.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2021-22: S5409 - Referred to education

2019-20: A8566 - Referred to education

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

TBD

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the first of July one year after the date
on which it shall have become a law.

summary: Creates a uniform presentation for students regarding applying for financial aid; directs students to complete an affidavit certifying that the student attended the presentation and stating whether the student intends to apply for financial aid.
